Published Sep 29, 2026, 7:03 AM EDT

Luc Haasbroek is a writer and videographer from Durban, South Africa. He has been writing professionally about pop culture for eight years. Luc's areas of interest are broad: he's just as passionate about psychology and history as he is about movies and TV. He's especially drawn to the places where these topics overlap.
Luc is also an avid producer of video essays and looks forward to expanding his writing career. When not writing, he can be found hiking, playing Dungeons & Dragons, hanging out with his cats, and doing deep dives on whatever topic happens to have captured his interest that week.

Every genre has its classics that all fans need to read, the foundational works that shaped our perception of them and impacted the culture as a whole. In science fiction's case, the masterpieces don't just imagine a possible future but strive to say something timeless about the human condition.

This list looks at some of the most essential sci-fi books, from the devastating psychological depth of Flowers for Algernon to the cyberpunk prophecy of Neuromancer. Calling any book perfect is asking for trouble, but these 10 certainly come close. Some transformed science fiction permanently; others simply demonstrate what the genre can accomplish when an exceptional writer pushes one great idea as far as it can go.

'The Forever War' (1974)

Image via St. Martin's Press

"Tonight we're going to show you eight silent ways to kill a man." In this one, author Joe Haldeman, himself a Vietnam veteran, introduces us to physicist William Mandella, who is conscripted into an elite force fighting the mysterious Taurans across interstellar space. Soldiers can travel enormous distances relatively quickly from their perspective, but relativity means decades or even centuries may pass on Earth while they're away.

Mandella survives a campaign lasting months, only to return home and discover that the society he fought to protect has become almost unrecognizable. While there is punchy action here and a bevy of cool futuristic tech, including stasis fields, power armor, and pods that resist extreme gravity, the focus is really on the protagonist's alienation. In other words, the hard sci-fi framework conceals a powerful, personal allegory about the lingering effects of combat.

'The Left Hand of Darkness' (1969)

Image via Ace Books

"I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination." This is another allegorical classic. In The Left Hand of Darkness, the main character, Genly Ai, travels to the frozen planet Gethen as an envoy of the Ekumen, hoping to persuade its nations to join an interstellar civilization. There, he experiences serious culture shock, as the inhabitants of Gethen are generally neither male nor female, becoming sexually differentiated only during periods of fertility.

Genly understands this intellectually, yet his assumptions about gender continually distort how he perceives the people around him. Author Ursula K. Le Guin (the brains behind the Earthsea fantasy novels) uses that premise to explore gender, politics, nationalism, communication, and the difficulty of seeing beyond one's cultural conditioning. That said, even aside from the themes, the novel is simply a touching story, particularly when it comes to Genly's relationship with the Gethen politician Estraven.

'What We Can Know' (2025)

Image via Jonathan Cape

"The past is not behind us. It is beneath us." This is the latest masterpiece from Atonement's Ian McEwan. In the 22nd century, academic Tom Metcalfe studies the lost world of the early 21st century and becomes fascinated by a famous poem that was supposedly read aloud at a dinner in 2014 before disappearing. His attempt to locate it gradually turns literary scholarship into something resembling detective work. It's a wonderful reversal of conventional historical fiction tropes, as well as a believable (occasionally frightening) vision of the future.

More than that, however, What We Can Know is really a portrait of our own mad moment in time. We see the present through Tom's eyes, meaning that its flaws and inconsistencies become glaringly obvious. At the same time, McEwan keeps rich characterization and personal drama (not to mention some juicy mysteries) front and center.

'Hyperion' (1989)

Image via Doubleday

"The Hegemony Consul sat on the balcony of his ebony spaceship and played Rachmaninoff's Prelude in C-sharp Minor." Hyperion focuses on seven pilgrims journeying to a distant world where the mysterious Time Tombs are moving backward through time and an almost mythical creature known as the Shrike waits among them. Each traveler has a deeply personal reason for making the journey, and the novel gradually reveals those reasons through a series of stories told along the way.

The structure famously echoes The Canterbury Tales, but writer Dan Simmons uses it to move effortlessly between different kinds of science fiction. One pilgrim's story plays like military sci-fi, another like a detective mystery, another like tragedy, another like horror. The result is a novel that keeps reinventing itself while steadily building its mythology. The Shrike is especially effective because it's never reduced to a conventional monster; rather, it exists somewhere between killer, god, devil, weapon, and cosmic mystery.

'The Dispossessed' (1974)

Image via Avon Books

"There was a wall. It did not look important." Ursula K. Le Guin strikes again; this is another compelling sci-fi story with strong political and social undercurrents. Physicist Shevek leaves the anarchist society of Anarres for the wealthy neighboring world of Urras. Anarres was founded by revolutionaries who rejected hierarchy and private property, while Urras contains wealth, inequality, and concentrated political power that looks far more familiar to modern readers.

Neither world, however, is presented as an uncomplicated answer to the problems of the other. That refusal to create an easy utopia is what makes the novel so enduring. Anarres is remarkably equal in many respects, yet totally stagnant in others. Urras, meanwhile, offers abundance and intellectual opportunity, but also resentment and deep social discord. Back in the mid-'70s, with the Cold War still underway, these sorts of debates were very much at the forefront of the public consciousness.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.

💊The Matrix

🔥Mad Max

🌧️Blade Runner

🏜️Dune

🚀Star Wars

TEST YOUR SURVIVAL →

01

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…

Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.

The Resistance, Zion

The Matrix

You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.

You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.

You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.

You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.

The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.

The Wasteland

Mad Max

The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.

You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.

You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.

You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.

In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.

Los Angeles, 2049

Blade Runner

You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.

You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.

In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.

You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.

In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.

Arrakis

Dune

Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.

Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.

You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.

Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.

In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.

You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.

You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.

You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.

In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

'Slaughterhouse-Five' (1969)

Image via Dell

"All this happened, more or less." Here, Kurt Vonnegut draws on his experiences as a POW who survived the bombing of Dresden, but he refuses to transform that trauma into a conventional war novel. Instead, his protagonist Billy Pilgrim becomes "unstuck in time," bouncing uncontrollably between different moments in his life: childhood, war, marriage, middle age, death, and even his supposed abduction by aliens from the planet Tralfamadore. The sci-fi elements initially seem almost absurd, but they become essential to the story.

Billy cannot leave the war behind because, from his perspective, the past never really becomes past; he can be a comfortable middle-aged man one moment and a terrified prisoner in Dresden the next. This eerie but fascinating approach is paralleled by the way the Tralfamadorians perceive every moment as permanently existing. Ultimately,Slaughterhouse-Five becomes an exploration of PTSD, coping mechanisms, memory, and free will.

'The Stars My Destination' (1956)

Image via Gollancz SF Masterworks

"He was one hundred and seventy days dying and not yet dead." Stranded aboard the wrecked Nomad, Gully Foyle sees another spacecraft pass close enough to rescue him. It doesn't. His resulting fury gives a previously directionless man a purpose: find the ship, discover why it abandoned him, and destroy everyone responsible. Alfred Bester takes the basic architecture of The Count of Monte Cristo and detonates it inside a futuristic society where humans have learned to "jaunte," teleporting themselves across enormous distances through thought alone.

Indeed, The Stars My Destination is fundamentally a revenge story encased in sci-fi trappings. The protagonist is brutal, obsessive, frequently repellent, and enormously compelling, despite (or perhaps because of) his deep moral grayness. Not to mention, on the stylistic front, the novel's experimental typography and psychedelic later passages also feel startlingly modern for a book published in 1956.

'Neuromancer' (1984)

Image via Ace Books

"The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel." Cyberpunk's center of gravity. Neuromancer centers on Case, a washed-up hacker whose nervous system has been deliberately damaged, leaving him unable to access cyberspace. An enigmatic employer offers to repair him in exchange for his participation in an extraordinarily dangerous job, pairing him with the lethally augmented mercenary Molly Millions. Together, they navigate a world of rogue AI and all-powerful corporations.

Here, author William Gibson seamlessly fuses high-tech with low-life, discarding the clean, optimistic spaceships of mid-20th century sci-fi for a gritty, neon-drenched, corporate-dominated dystopia. He innovated in all sorts of ways, even coining the term cyberspace itself. Much of his vision looks uncomfortably prescient now. Gibson's writing is also great on a sentence-by-sentence level here: the prose is noirish, hyperkinetic, and frequently poetic.

'Dune' (1965)

Image via Chilton Books

"A beginning is the time for taking the most delicate care that the balances are correct." Dune remains one of sci-fi's absolute high points when it comes to worldbuilding. With it, Frank Herbert created a universe whose politics, religion, ecology, economics, warfare, and mythology are tightly interlocked. Spice enables interstellar civilization, which makes control of the desert planet Arrakis politically indispensable. Likewise, the planet's brutal ecology shapes Fremen culture, while their religious beliefs have themselves been manipulated by outside powers.

It's against that colorful backdrop that the messianic cautionary tale of Paul Atreides plays out. He is soon entangled in realpolitik involving the Fremen, House Harkonnen, the Emperor, and the shadowy Bene Gesserit. Along the way, Herbert gives readers many of the pleasures of a grand adventure, like duels, betrayals, political maneuvering, enormous battles, and giant alien beasts, while also quietly interrogating the very fantasy of the chosen hero.

'Flowers for Algernon' (1966)

Image via Mariner Books Classics

"Dr Strauss says I shoud rite down what I think and remembir and every thing that happins to me from now on." This is one of the most heartbreaking works of soft sci-fi ever written. In Flowers for Algernon, Charlie Gordon, an intellectually disabled man, undergoes an experimental procedure designed to dramatically increase his intelligence. His progress reports initially contain simple vocabulary and frequent spelling mistakes, but as the treatment works, the language itself transforms.

Luc Haasbroek is a writer and videographer from Durban, South Africa. He has been writing professionally about pop culture for eight years. Luc's areas of interest are broad: he's just as passionate about psychology and history as he is about movies and TV. He's especially drawn to the places where these topics overlap.
Luc is also an avid producer of video essays and looks forward to expanding his writing career. When not writing, he can be found hiking, playing Dungeons & Dragons, hanging out with his cats, and doing deep dives on whatever topic happens to have captured his interest that week.

Every genre has its classics that all fans need to read, the foundational works that shaped our perception of them and impacted the culture as a whole. In science fiction's case, the masterpieces don't just imagine a possible future but strive to say something timeless about the human condition.

This list looks at some of the most essential sci-fi books, from the devastating psychological depth of Flowers for Algernon to the cyberpunk prophecy of Neuromancer. Calling any book perfect is asking for trouble, but these 10 certainly come close. Some transformed science fiction permanently; others simply demonstrate what the genre can accomplish when an exceptional writer pushes one great idea as far as it can go.
'The Forever War' (1974)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/the-forever-war-1974-joe-haldeman.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The cover of the novel The Forever War

blocks.x: Image via St. Martin's Press

"Tonight we're going to show you eight silent ways to kill a man." In this one, author Joe Haldeman, himself a Vietnam veteran, introduces us to physicist William Mandella, who is conscripted into an elite force fighting the mysterious Taurans across interstellar space. Soldiers can travel enormous distances relatively quickly from their perspective, but relativity means decades or even centuries may pass on Earth while they're away.

Mandella survives a campaign lasting months, only to return home and discover that the society he fought to protect has become almost unrecognizable. While there is punchy action here and a bevy of cool futuristic tech, including stasis fields, power armor, and pods that resist extreme gravity, the focus is really on the protagonist's alienation. In other words, the hard sci-fi framework conceals a powerful, personal allegory about the lingering effects of combat.
'The Left Hand of Darkness' (1969)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/the-hainish-cycle-ursula-k-le-guin.png?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The cover of the novel The Left Hand of Darkness by Ursula K. Le Guin

blocks.x: Image via Ace Books

"I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination." This is another allegorical classic. In The Left Hand of Darkness, the main character, Genly Ai, travels to the frozen planet Gethen as an envoy of the Ekumen, hoping to persuade its nations to join an interstellar civilization. There, he experiences serious culture shock, as the inhabitants of Gethen are generally neither male nor female, becoming sexually differentiated only during periods of fertility.

Genly understands this intellectually, yet his assumptions about gender continually distort how he perceives the people around him. Author Ursula K. Le Guin (the brains behind the Earthsea fantasy novels) uses that premise to explore gender, politics, nationalism, communication, and the difficulty of seeing beyond one's cultural conditioning. That said, even aside from the themes, the novel is simply a touching story, particularly when it comes to Genly's relationship with the Gethen politician Estraven.
'What We Can Know' (2025)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/what-we-can-know-book0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: What We Can Know Book cover

blocks.x: Image via Jonathan Cape

"The past is not behind us. It is beneath us." This is the latest masterpiece from Atonement's Ian McEwan. In the 22nd century, academic Tom Metcalfe studies the lost world of the early 21st century and becomes fascinated by a famous poem that was supposedly read aloud at a dinner in 2014 before disappearing. His attempt to locate it gradually turns literary scholarship into something resembling detective work. It's a wonderful reversal of conventional historical fiction tropes, as well as a believable (occasionally frightening) vision of the future.

More than that, however, What We Can Know is really a portrait of our own mad moment in time. We see the present through Tom's eyes, meaning that its flaws and inconsistencies become glaringly obvious. At the same time, McEwan keeps rich characterization and personal drama (not to mention some juicy mysteries) front and center.
'Hyperion' (1989)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/hyperion-1989-dan-simmons.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The cover of the novel Hyperion

blocks.x: Image via Doubleday

"The Hegemony Consul sat on the balcony of his ebony spaceship and played Rachmaninoff's Prelude in C-sharp Minor." Hyperion focuses on seven pilgrims journeying to a distant world where the mysterious Time Tombs are moving backward through time and an almost mythical creature known as the Shrike waits among them. Each traveler has a deeply personal reason for making the journey, and the novel gradually reveals those reasons through a series of stories told along the way.

The structure famously echoes The Canterbury Tales, but writer Dan Simmons uses it to move effortlessly between different kinds of science fiction. One pilgrim's story plays like military sci-fi, another like a detective mystery, another like tragedy, another like horror. The result is a novel that keeps reinventing itself while steadily building its mythology. The Shrike is especially effective because it's never reduced to a conventional monster; rather, it exists somewhere between killer, god, devil, weapon, and cosmic mystery.
'The Dispossessed' (1974)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/the-dispossessed-1974.png?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Avon Books

"There was a wall. It did not look important." Ursula K. Le Guin strikes again; this is another compelling sci-fi story with strong political and social undercurrents. Physicist Shevek leaves the anarchist society of Anarres for the wealthy neighboring world of Urras. Anarres was founded by revolutionaries who rejected hierarchy and private property, while Urras contains wealth, inequality, and concentrated political power that looks far more familiar to modern readers.

Neither world, however, is presented as an uncomplicated answer to the problems of the other. That refusal to create an easy utopia is what makes the novel so enduring. Anarres is remarkably equal in many respects, yet totally stagnant in others. Urras, meanwhile, offers abundance and intellectual opportunity, but also resentment and deep social discord. Back in the mid-'70s, with the Cold War still underway, these sorts of debates were very much at the forefront of the public consciousness.

'Slaughterhouse-Five' (1969)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/slaughterhouse-five-kurt-vonnegut-delacorte-press.png?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2

"All this happened, more or less." Here, Kurt Vonnegut draws on his experiences as a POW who survived the bombing of Dresden, but he refuses to transform that trauma into a conventional war novel. Instead, his protagonist Billy Pilgrim becomes "unstuck in time," bouncing uncontrollably between different moments in his life: childhood, war, marriage, middle age, death, and even his supposed abduction by aliens from the planet Tralfamadore. The sci-fi elements initially seem almost absurd, but they become essential to the story.

Billy cannot leave the war behind because, from his perspective, the past never really becomes past; he can be a comfortable middle-aged man one moment and a terrified prisoner in Dresden the next. This eerie but fascinating approach is paralleled by the way the Tralfamadorians perceive every moment as permanently existing. https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/the-stars-my-destination0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1

"He was one hundred and seventy days dying and not yet dead." Stranded aboard the wrecked Nomad, Gully Foyle sees another spacecraft pass close enough to rescue him. It doesn't. Alfred Bester takes the basic architecture of The Count of Monte Cristo and detonates it inside a futuristic society where humans have learned to "jaunte," teleporting themselves across enormous distances through thought alone.

Indeed, The Stars My Destination is fundamentally a revenge story encased in sci-fi trappings. The protagonist is brutal, obsessive, frequently repellent, and enormously compelling, despite (or perhaps because of) his deep moral grayness. Not to mention, on the stylistic front, the novel's experimental typography and psychedelic later passages also feel startlingly modern for a book published in 1956.

https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/neuromancer-1.png?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1

"The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel." Cyberpunk's center of gravity. Neuromancer centers on Case, a washed-up hacker whose nervous system has been deliberately damaged, leaving him unable to access cyberspace. An enigmatic employer offers to repair him in exchange for his participation in an extraordinarily dangerous job, pairing him with the lethally augmented mercenary Molly Millions. Together, they navigate a world of rogue AI and all-powerful corporations.

Here, author William Gibson seamlessly fuses high-tech with low-life, discarding the clean, optimistic spaceships of mid-20th century sci-fi for a gritty, neon-drenched, corporate-dominated dystopia. He innovated in all sorts of ways, even coining the term cyberspace itself. Much of his vision looks uncomfortably prescient now. Gibson's writing is also great on a sentence-by-sentence level here: the prose is noirish, hyperkinetic, and frequently poetic.

Likewise, the planet's brutal ecology shapes Fremen culture, while their religious beliefs have themselves been manipulated by outside powers.

It's against that colorful backdrop that the messianic cautionary tale of Paul Atreides plays out. He is soon entangled in realpolitik involving the Fremen, House Harkonnen, the Emperor, and the shadowy Bene Gesserit. items.summary: It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One,
items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

items.text:
Happy this week all! ...Ugh, you are all still here. When I went on holiday last week, I was hoping that I'd return to find that the whole "videogame journalism career" thing was just a fleeting delusion brought on by excess consumption of unripe pears. Perhaps I've actually been a wealthy gentleman gadabout this whole time, free of any need to keep the hellmouth topped up with layoff reports in order to stave off deprivation and disaster.

The one consolation - other than EIC Julian's many encouraging facial expressions and hand gestures – is that people are still making new PC games, and a few of them are actually quite interesting! Here's the latest list of new releases.

Monday 28th September

No, I refuse to believe that my holiday is over. Let's all get the heck down to Camp Whittlewood, a pixelart horror RPG about cub scouts going camping in the deep forest, featuring absolutely no serial killers.

Camp Whittlewood aside, there are precious few holiday-themed games on this list. Instead, we have games like HR: Human Remains. It's about being an office clerk in Hell, after humans lost a war with the demons. Get through your to-do list, or get fed to the Maw (no relation).

Yots is a PS1-ified co-op extraction game in which you repeatedly pillage a procgen city that looks like Silent Hill, assuming Silent Hill existed in the 1930s. I'm pretty sure it did. I don't think they had Pyramid Head technology back then, but they certainly had fog.

Speaking of lumbering metal monsters - where are my 90s Mechwarrior enjoyers? Drop Command is here with a mixture of cockpit combat and overarching 4X elements.

Tuesday 29th September

Nivalis Nights is a cyberpunk restaurant management game and life sim from the makers of Cloudpunk. The views should be pretty lush, whatever you may think of the jobbing element. Alas, my holiday!

Toem 2 is the new toem' up from John Toem, developer of Toem. (Actual studio name: Something We Made. Actual game description: a gentle diorama platformer and photography puzzler.)

Transport Fever 3 is the latest borderline masturbatory infrastructure meddler from Paradox, featuring the shiniest trains you ever did see.

From the makers of Human Fall Flat, here's Tiny Flock, a VR shepherding sim with more seesaws, circus machines and great white sharks than I believe is traditional, in real-life shepherding.

Wednesday 30th September

Radiosol casts you as a mechanical spider exploring a fallen world of attractively dusty and dessicated megastructures. It does use genAI to translate the game into Spanish, Japanese, German, French, and Chinese. I am underlining my own reminder to write/commission a piece on genAI translation in gamedev.

Okko The Exiled is a pretty gorgeous 2D sidescroller about some diminutive fellow with horns and a massive club. Look at him go!

Songs of Glimmerwick is a witch school RPG in which magic and music are closely allied. The developers are promising "hijinks". Don't… tempt me, Frodo!

Crusader Kings 3: By God Alone is the CK3 expansion in which you can run the Vatican and do all kinds of notionally un-Christian things – just ask Julian.

Thursday 1st October

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is an Unreal Engineered revamp of the early noughties musou masher and its Xtreme Legends expandalone. Always had a sneaking fondness for DW games, despite the fact that they often play like lawnmower simulators in which the grass consists of shrieking spear guys.

RetroSpace (pictured) is the immersive sim with Saturday Night Fever vibes in which you, a janitor, try to survive inside a space station that has been yoinked into a blackhole.

There are planes in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Bamco's latest Hot Shots-alike.

Friday 2nd October

What's the weather like there? On-going UK drought notwithstanding, we're edging into the golden season where you still get a few immaculate summer skies, but elegantly merged with the crispness and enchantment of autumn. Argh, having to undertake 'gainful employment' in these conditions is an offence to Nature. Now is the time to be out of doors, cavorting in the leaves, rather than staying inside to play/write about smelly videogames. Although if you have any new releases to recommend, we'd be interested as ever. Have a jolly week.

items.text:
In the early 2000s, Brad Pitt—between peaks in pure movie-star power—was attached to a Coen brothers adaptation of To The White Sea, a survival novel from James Dickey. The story from the author of Deliverance follows a World War II tailgunner shot down over Japan who must make his way to safety from enemy territory. The movie would feature almost no dialogue, as Pitt’s character did not speak Japanese and would spend much of his time on a defensive killing spree anyway. It would have been an ambitious undertaking for both the Coens and Pitt, but after a few years of push-pull between star, studio, and filmmakers, the movie was never made.


Heart Of The Beast is not exactly a reincarnation of that project. But Pitt’s new movie does feel like a new chance for him to finally try out a dialogue-light survival story featuring sometimes-gruesome violence. If anything, there are even fewer characters in Heart Of The Beast than To The White Sea would have had; veteran James Belmont (Pitt) only encounters a single human before crashing his small plane into the Alaskan wilderness. But Beast has significantly more chat, because James spends a considerable amount of time talking to his dog, a fellow combat vet who accompanies him on the harrowing journey. While David Ayer’s film was likely less expensive than the Coens’ film, its existence underlines the fact that Pitt may, if anything, be a bigger star in 2026 than he was 25 years earlier. Despite the occasional flop, he’s been instrumental to the success of movies like Bullet Train and F1. Heart Of The Beast seems likely to continue that streak, but it’s also the latest Pitt project to almost willfully misunderstand his abilities as an actor.

To The White Sea would have represented a particular challenge for the Pitt of 2002. Though he played plenty of beautiful brooders in his youth, his grabbiest roles tended to be his gabbiest: the hothead cop in Seven who can’t stop asking what’s in the box, the institutionalized rich-boy radical in 12 Monkeys, and the monologuing Tyler Durden in Fight Club. All that smartass and/or dumbass dialogue, all that gesticulating with his hands; it doesn’t seem coincidental that Steven Soderbergh, who delights in breaking actors’ habits, directed him to deadpan, fry-munching minimalism in Ocean’s Eleven.


That ensemble romp was Pitt’s only really big hit of the early 2000s, with George Clooney, Julia Roberts, and Matt Damon sharing the credit. Similarly, some of his minor face-savers like The Mexican and Spy Game were aided by at least one other mega-famous name. To The White Sea supposedly fell apart due to budget concerns; it seems possible that Pitt on his own, especially sans dialogue, was not considered enough to sell a big-budget movie. By the time he found his way back to the Coens for 2008’s Burn After Reading, Pitt had clocked in for a couple of big hits like Troy and Mr. And Mrs. Smith, burnishing his commercial reputation. But he also appeared to rededicate himself to interrogating his now-middle-aged masculinity.


Burn After Reading presents the most broadly cartoonish version of this, with Pitt as a buffoonish gym rat whose gruesome demise becomes an exquisitely timed punchline; today, his presence as that character also reads like a savaging of handsome actors who make buffing up for a big role their whole personality. But Pitt’s refraction of masculine norms shines through a less spoofy lens in films like The Assassination Of Jesse James By The Coward Robert Ford, where he plays the legendary outlaw as an ornery, unstable killer; The Tree Of Life, which casts him an imposing, perpetually frustrated father in the 1940s; and The Counselor, where he’s a shady businessman who speaks with authority but can only shrug fatalistically when presented with a horrific mistake. Pitt’s more traditional movie-star turns from this period also feel less insistent about his man’s-man bona fides, to the point where in The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button, a romantic and Oscar-nominated star role, he’s quite literally recessive.


Even his work for Quentin Tarantino in Once Upon A Time…In Hollywood, clearly celebratory of Pitt’s masculine bravado, complicates any sense of pure glorification: His stuntman Cliff Booth, whom he’s about to reprise for a years-later sequel, is a likable scrub. He lives in a trailer, cooks himself boxed mac and cheese, does odd jobs, and upon recalling the fight with Bruce Lee that got him kicked off a studio lot, he can only shrug and offer a self-amused “fair enough.” He’s also so confident in his masculinity, in his middle-aged shirtlessness and his lot in life, that those moments of showboating—fighting Bruce Lee, taking on the Manson gang—only happen in short bursts between his laconic observations.


Pitt won an Oscar for the film, which was, in many ways, the culmination of a decade-plus of work that seemed to be done without much concern for box office glory. Doubtless there were certain commercial calculations at play, but Pitt appeared to use his most blatantly mainstream films like World War Z to keep his line of credit going for tough, well-honed movies like Killing Them Softly. What, then, to make of the subsequent and fairly dire planes/trains/automobiles trilogy of Heart Of The Beast, Bullet Train, and F1? They’re watchable, and yes, F1 was nominated for Best Picture. But besides placing Pitt on a series of vehicles, the main thing they have in common is an oppressive self-consciousness about what a quietly macho guy Pitt can be. Rather than emboldening him, his Oscar seems to have convinced him that his best is no longer necessary.


It’s not that Pitt isn’t up to the task of playing a haunted, taciturn, dog-loving military man in Heart Of The Beast. He’s convincing enough to fudge the fact that his character would have been pretty old for active duty in the 2000s-era Middle East conflicts, and he’s charismatic enough to hold the screen for the extended periods where it’s just him and a dog. (The dog isn’t acting, per se, but has some built-in expressiveness that makes him a surprisingly strong scene partner.) But at his age, even playing a character who suffers some pretty intense physical setbacks, assuming a tough stoicism feels a little more like cosplay than acting. When he recalls shooting an enemy combatant in the head as payback for injuring his dog, Pitt doesn’t add much dimension to the recollection. Throughout the film, he seems mournful primarily about the fact that his dog has been through hell on the battlefield, conveyed with a tone that vaguely implies that the dog nobly volunteered for duty. A better movie might have drawn a subtle connection to the simultaneous dehumanization of war and humanization of our animal friends. But whenever the movie strays beyond the mechanics of survival, Ayer and Pitt keep it squarely in Support The Troops mode.


If this were a one-off, the way that Pitt’s previous Ayer movie Fury seemed vaguely anomalous back in 2014, it might be easy enough to dismiss as something that interests Pitt without necessarily challenging him. Plenty of actors have those little hang-ups, and on the Ayer scale of violent machismo, Heart Of The Beast practically qualifies as gentle. Pitt, though, has apparently decided to make movies and non-characters like this a bigger part of his star persona. F1 in particular plays like an I-want-one-too vehicle of middle-age reaffirmation in the vein of Top Gun: Maverick, right down to poaching that film’s ultra-efficient technician-director Joseph Kosinski to showcase an aging star proving that he’s still the best in the biz.


Whatever you think of Maverick or Tom Cruise, that movie draws upon the cultural memory of the original Top Gun. F1, on the other hand, seems nostalgic for a Brad Pitt who never really existed—for an idea of the star as a paragon of professional but stubbornly individualistic masculinity. GQ Pitt and Esquire Pitt, maybe, but not movie Pitt, like a version of his Cliff Booth scrubbed of the nastiness and moral ambiguity. Similarly, the kind of easy shorthand Pitt seeks in Heart Of The Beast seems to refer to a combination of his work in the World War II movies Inglourious Basterds (which ultimately downplays his badassery) and Fury (which plays it way up). Then there’s Bullet Train and Wolfs, Pitt’s already-forgotten streaming re-team with Clooney, which take an even more piffling approach to putting Pitt back in action. But they still focus intently on Pitt as a singular and unusually badass man, with all the dimensionality of a cameo where he plays himself, somehow distended to feature-length. (Perhaps not coincidentally, he does have cameos in The Lost City and Deadpool 2, albeit not quite playing himself.)


Given what’s been made public about Pitt’s personal life, it’s difficult to avoid reading Pitt’s recent professional choices as something happening in concert with his blemished image, maybe even because of it. The public, plainly, seems not to care much (or, perhaps, know much) about the allegations that Pitt abused two of his children as well as Jolie. Pitt himself, though, must understand the potential for him to wind up closer to Mel Gibson or Johnny Depp (who, despite various efforts to whitewash or ignore various misdeeds, haven’t been able to hold on to the same cachet) than, say, Tom Cruise (who still commands A-list projects). Pitt’s recent work feels like an actor playing defense, and with far less go-for-broke conviction than someone like Cruise has shown in order to half-justify his messianic impulses.


Pitt has never positioned himself as quite so superhuman. Though he may not have a signature character as wrenchingly emotive as Cruise’s Frank T.J. Mackey from Magnolia, he sometimes affects a Robert Redford-like combination of sensitivity and pointed callowness, befitting his early work with the man himself on A River Runs Through It. Where his best performances might actually outdo Redford is his depiction of half-sublimated male rage, his new movies feel like the product of belatedly deciding that maybe it’s better to finish the job of sublimating that toxicity, lest its emergence draw uncomfortable parallels to Pitt’s real life. Hence no more bullying, dissatisfied father types as in Tree Of Life, or damaged-goods son types as in Ad Astra. It’s better, apparently, to associate his masculinity—and any detestable real-life decisions it may involve—with military-grade stoicism or last-athlete-standing individuality.


It’s also possible that Pitt is simply and cynically acknowledging the end of his road as a more actorly brand of movie star, something not many stars can much afford these days—quite literally, given that Pitt’s last really strong performance, in the death-and-rebirth-of-Hollywood epic Babylon, was a spectacular box office flop. In that film, Pitt’s Jack Conrad is a silent-film star who makes a go of maintaining his lofty position in a post-talkie world, only to meet with bad reviews and fading audience interest. Not consoled by a gossip columnist’s argument that while his time is over, he will achieve a form of immortality through the work that has already been done, a despondent Jack eventually dies by suicide.


Nothing so drastic awaits the real Pitt. It’s an underrated aspect of Hollywood’s age-defiance habit; actors are no longer expected to retire or simply see the work dry up when they hit 50. It may be that the second Cliff Booth movie will put Pitt back in touch with a sense of human frailty alongside his barely diminished ability to look cool as hell. If not, maybe another movie will; his near-peer Cruise is stepping back from the brink of action oblivion with Digger (though F1 seems to have dared him into doing a Days Of Thunder sequel). At the moment, though, Pitt is putting the thinned-out version of his image first, as if he’s realized that he prefers the magazine-profile version of himself over whatever he’s revealed through his best performances.

Arthur Morgan Actor Officially Addresses One of 'Red Dead Redemption 2's Biggest Fan Theories [Exclusive]

Image via Rockstar Games

Dutch van der Linde gives Red Dead Redemption 2 players plenty of reasons to wonder when he lost his way. As the Van der Linde gang falls apart, its leader grows increasingly ruthless, and the failed trolley robbery offers one possible explanation. Did Dutch change after hitting his head, or had Arthur Morgan and John Marston been following a man who was capable of those choices all along? It is a debate fans can revisit every time they play through the gang’s final months. Roger Clark, who played Arthur, has his own answer, and it places far more weight on the people around Dutch than on any injury.

When asked about the trolley theory during a Red Dead Redemption panel moderated by Collider's Maggie Lovitt at FanX Salt Lake Comic & Pop Culture Convention with Clark and John Marston actor Rob Wiethoff, Clark did not leave much room for doubt. “I disagree. I don’t believe in that at all,” Clark said. He pointed to Dutch’s killing of Heidi McCourt, an innocent bystander whose death predates the trolley crash. For Clark, that makes it difficult to pin Dutch’s cruelty on a single blow to the head, even if the robbery comes at a point when his behavior is becoming harder for the gang to excuse.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Western Icon Are You Most Like?
No Name · Doc Holliday · Wyatt Earp · Mattie Ross

Pick your name, your gun, your horse and how you spend a night in town, and we will tell you which legend of the Old West you would have been. Four icons are waiting at the end of this: the stranger who never gives his name, the gambler who would die for a friend, the lawman who never wanted the badge, and the girl nobody has ever talked out of anything.

🚬No Name(Dollars Trilogy)

🃏Doc Holliday(Tombstone)

⭐Wyatt Earp(Tombstone)

🐎Mattie Ross(True Grit)

FIND YOUR ICON →

01

The town is about to learn your name. What do they call you?
In a Western, what people call you is already half the character.

AThey never do find it out, so the stranger will have to do.
BA nickname I picked up at a card table and never shook off.
CMarshal, and most people say it with a bit of respect.
DMy full name, and I will correct anybody who tries to shorten it.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What are you carrying?
Everything out here is character, right down to what is sitting on your hip.

AOne revolver I have had for years and have never once talked about.
BA pistol, a knife and a deck of cards, and the cards do most of the damage.
CA shotgun, because it tends to end arguments rather than start them.
DMy father's gun, which is far too big for me, and I am carrying it anyway.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What are you riding?
A hero and their horse is one of the oldest relationships in cinema.

ASomething plain that nobody in town would look at twice.
BWhatever I won last night, which may not be strictly mine yet.
CA big steady horse that will not spook when things get loud.
DA pony I overpaid for and named myself, and I will hear nothing against him.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

You have got one evening in town. How does it go?
The saloon is where these films quietly tell you who somebody really is.

AOne drink at the far end of the bar with my back to the wall.
BAt the card table, holding court, up forty dollars and climbing.
CA quick drink, then a walk round town to see that everything is quiet.
DUpstairs with the ledger, working out exactly what tomorrow is going to cost.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

A stranger offers you money for a job that sounds like trouble.
Somebody always turns up with a full purse and a bad idea.

AI ask how much, and then I ask for a good deal more than that.
BI say yes before he has finished, mostly because it sounds like a story.
CI ask him who gets hurt if I turn him down.
DI ask for the terms in writing before anybody shakes on anything.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody is waiting for you in the street. What does the town see?
Two people, an empty road, and everybody else watching from behind the shutters.

ASomebody walking out very slowly who has not said a single word.
BSomebody grinning, which everyone watching finds deeply unnerving.
CSomebody making one last attempt to talk the other man down.
DSomebody far too young to be out there, walking out regardless.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What is the one thing you will not do out here?
The code is about the only thing west of the river that actually holds.

AExplain myself to somebody who has not earned an explanation.
BRide off and leave a friend standing out there on his own.
CLet a whole town pay for a fight it had nothing to do with.
DLet a grown man tell me I am too young to be standing here.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

The job is finished. Where does the story leave you?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your icon.

AOn a ridge somewhere, riding away, without saying goodbye to anybody.
BSomewhere warm and worn out, having enjoyed very nearly all of it.
CHome, with the badge on the table and the whole thing behind me.
DOlder, changed by it, and telling this story for the rest of my life.

REVEAL MY ICON →

The Dust Has Settled
Your Western Icon Is…

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble.
This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

The Dollars Trilogy · 1964–1966

The Man With No Name

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to,
because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room
without you ever having to mention it.

Eastwood built the character out of everything he refused to do, stripping away the
backstory, the speeches and every bit of reassurance until only the competence was left.

You keep your own counsel, and while other people occasionally find that unnerving, you
have never felt any real need to fix it for them.

The Dollars films work because he genuinely is in it for himself right up until the
moment he is not, and he never explains that part either.

You would be gone before anybody got a chance to thank you.

Doc Holliday · Tombstone · 1993

Doc Holliday

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal
person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two
things were in any tension.

Doc has no real reason to be in this fight beyond the fact that his friend is in it,
which is the only reason he has ever needed for anything.

You lead with wit, and it does a very effective job of hiding how seriously you take the
handful of people you actually care about.

Val Kilmer's performance is the most quoted in the entire genre because the jokes keep
getting sharper as the situation gets worse.

You would spend everything you had on this and still describe it as a good week.

Wyatt Earp · Tombstone · 1993

Wyatt Earp

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the
alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most
Western reason there has ever been.

Earp is the reluctant authority figure, a man who came to town specifically to be left
alone and somehow ended up answerable for all of it.

You are protective by instinct, so when something goes wrong your first thought is who
is exposed rather than who is to blame.

These films understand that keeping order costs far more than breaking it, and that the
person holding the line almost never gets thanked.

You would do the whole thing again, and you would complain about it the entire time.

Mattie Ross · True Grit · 1969 & 2010

Mattie Ross

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had
already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

Mattie is the most relentless character in the Western canon and she manages it through
argument, paperwork and flat refusal rather than a fast draw.

You have no patience for being managed, so you negotiate, you check the details and you
turn up exactly when you said you would.

True Grit is the rare Western where the moral centre is the youngest person on screen
and every adult around her has to catch up.

You would get what you came for, and the film is honest about what that takes out of
you.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

Roger Clark Thinks Hosea and Micah Tell Us More About Dutch Than the Trolley Does

Image via Rockstar Games

“I think the trolley had nothing to do with it,” Clark said. “I think Hosea leaving the gang had more to do with it.” He described Hosea Matthews as the angel on Dutch’s shoulder and Micah Bell as the devil who took his place. In Clark’s view, Micah did not create a new Dutch so much as give him room to act on impulses Hosea had helped keep in check. That reading makes Dutch’s downfall harder to pin to one scene. Clark said the question of whether Dutch was always like this or declined over time is part of what makes him interesting, and he suspects the answer is “a bit of both.” He also stressed that Dutch begins Red Dead Redemption 2 as a leader who cares about his people, which makes the gang’s collapse more painful to watch. “I don’t think it was one moment,” Clark said. “I think it’s lots of little small moments piled up on top of each other that change us.”

The trolley crash may be an easy moment to point to, but Clark sees Dutch’s choices, Hosea’s absence, and Micah’s influence as a much more revealing explanation. Stay tuned at Collider for more.

Published Sep 29, 2026, 5:12 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

No doubt, 2026 will be the year dedicated to Grand Theft Auto VI. With time getting ever closer to that tasty November 19 release date, the excitement among fans is palpable. Rockstar Games are about to deliver the biggest and possibly most profitable entertainment experience of all time and if the recent Netflix reveal is anything to go by, they're set to deliver in spades! But what comes next? Once the dust settles on Grand Theft Auto VI, what will Rockstar Games do next? Red Dead Redemption 3 perhaps or Bully 2? Well one leaker seems to have the answer . . . and it's a doozy.

A renowned leaker over on GTAforums has let slip what they claim to know as the next game coming out from Rockstar Games after Grand Theft Auto VI. Leaks occur all the time and taking the information with a pinch of salt is essential, but this one might be correct. Reason being, Shahanshah made claims about Grand Theft Auto VI way back in 2003 and most of them appear to be correct based on official reveals recently. If they truly have insider information, then their claim about Rockstars' next game is certainly not something to scoff at.

Source: Rockstar Games

Set in San Francisco and somewhere between 1968 and 1974, Rockstar Games' next game after Grand Theft Auto VI is predicted to be a sequel to L.A. Noire. It's not expected to release until 2030, giving Rockstar Games plenty of time to earn truck loads of cash from Grand Theft Auto VI and GTA Online across all the platforms before focussing on L.A. Noire 2. With Cole Phelps' story well and truly concluded, this new tale will take place decades later and focus on the Zodiac Killer murders of the late 60s.

With the original game having such a focus on face scanning and having gameplay mechanics hinging on facial expressions and tells, the sequel is set to take all this technology to the next level. According to the leaker, Rockstar Games are aiming for L.A. Noire 2 to be the best looking game ever made. Of course, if it's set in San Francisco, it most likely won't be called L.A. Noire 2, but it will be a successor and sequel to the 2011 detective drama that sold over 7.5 million copies during its lifetime.

Although most Rockstar Games' fans were hoping to see Red Dead Redemption 3 sooner rather than later, an L.A. Noire sequel is still very welcome. Upon hearing the news, most fans are overjoyed at the prospect of a sequel to L.A. Noire and hopeful that the leaks are true. Over on X, commentors had the following to say about the leaked news:

Please let this be true. LA Noir was a masterpiece.

And:

Thought a Max Payne sequel (not talking about the coming remakes) would be next, but this sounds even better, hope this is true

While another addressed the time left to wait until a 2030 release:

Zodiac killer story + LA noire?! Worth the wait.

Not all gamers were as optimistic though and some are struggling to beleive that the leak might be true. One such commentor said the following:

2030 is impossible. Rockstar is finishing GTA 6 and will launch its multiplayer spin-off next year. squeezing out a brand-new game while supporting GTA 6 and Online in a span of 3 years is impossible for Rockstar

And another:

No way R* will make a game outside of GTA lol. They cancelled all the GTA5 SP DLCs for Online. Only reason why they made RDR2 was to milk it’s online and it failed hard. R* themselves won’t make a SP game at most outsource the IP like they did with Remedy’s Mad Payne remakes.

Whether the leak is to be believed or not remains to be seen and until we hear something from official channels, it's up to the fans to speculate. But with amazing games still to come in 2026 and beyond, there's a lot to distract us gamers while we wait to hear more from Rockstar Games. Me personally, I'd like to see another Max Payne game set in a retirement home with an older Michael De Santa and Trevor Philips as Max's roommates. That might even blow Grand Theft Auto VI out of the water. We can but dream!

items.text:
Ys X: Nordics came out in Japan on September 28, 2023. As a big Ys lover in the U.S., I was stuck seeing screenshots, videos, and discussion of the game in Japanese all over the place, but not being able to play it myself. Though I managed to avoid spoilers, there was a sense when it finally hit the States on October 25 of the following year that the game was already an old one, and thus less exciting to discuss. The same thing happened when its updated version, Proud Nordics, dropped on July 31, 2025 in Japan, and February 20, 2026 over here. Sucks!

Most companies don’t do these sorts of staggered releases anymore, but Nippon Ichi Software and its international subsidiary, NIS America, still do for some of their published titles. But that might finally be changing. At PAX West, I spoke to Nippon Ichi CEO and recently appointed NIS America President Kenzo Saruhashi about why the company has been so slow to adopt simultaneous releases. Sure, localization takes time, but most companies nowadays can take that into account and have a release date planned that ensures that work has been done by the time it comes around. Not so for many of NIS America’s published games.

In the past, Saruhashi says, Nippon Ichi and NIS America operated more as two separate companies rather than a subsidiary and a parent company. By uniting them both under his primary leadership, he wants to see that change. To him, that means bringing more games in general west (right now, many of Nippon Ichi’s releases don’t make it to the States), but also bringing them here simultaneously with their Japanese release.

“In the past, a lot of it has been that in many ways we didn’t really have the deciding power to say, ‘We’re going to move forward with the goal of a simultaneous launch’ because we were almost operating as two separate companies,” Saruhashi says. “But now we can really say, [we’re operating] as a whole. And so, there are other factors such as resources and other physical impediments that make it difficult to do a simulship, of course, but I think we’re slowly, gradually able to close that gap thanks to our ability to work a little bit more [cooperatively] as companies.”

Saruhashi tells me that he sees a greater appetite than there used to be for Japanese games in the West, and for Western games in Japan. “Those walls are really coming down, and it feels like it doesn’t really matter so much where the game was made.”

Still, Saruhashi is taking a more direct role over the U.S. division of the company at a tough time for the U.S. and its games industry. I mention the struggles: tariffs, rising costs, chip shortages, layoffs, games flopping, studios closing. While there’s nothing to suggest NIS America is in any danger, it’s still a rough time to be operating over here. Does this impact his business at all? Saruhashi repeatedly tells me it does not.

“So the situation is quite a bit different in the sense that Japanese companies, they don’t really lay off their employees,” he says. “People tend to be lifelong employees of the company most of the time. Now part of that has to do with laws being different in Japan for one thing, but also there’s just a sort of a different cultural thought process about work and your relationship with work and so everyone comes to work with a mindset of: I’m going to be with this company for the rest of my life and I want to contribute to that success, and that helps reflect on me. So I think that may be a part of the discrepancy there.

“There’s also this feeling like, we have a tendency that we want to help people grow and develop within the company and so it’s been a long-standing thing where whether what the Company is doing is profitable, not profitable, it doesn’t really affect our decisions as much in Japan. A lot of companies still have that old-fashioned mindset which I personally am a fan of, but in recent years that’s becoming less and less of a thing in Japan which I feel a little sad about honestly.”

I also spoke with Saruhashi about whether or not the company was using generative AI in development, and his feelings on PlayStation discontinuing physical discs in 2028.

items.title: Climbers race against time, the elements, and each other for The Last First: Winter K2
items.author: Jacob Oller
items.summary: Just as the prevalence and clarity of satellite imagery has cleared the magical uncertainty from the obscure corners of the globe, so too have the highest
items.text:
Just as the prevalence and clarity of satellite imagery has cleared the magical uncertainty from the obscure corners of the globe, so too have the highest points of the world lost some of their unattainable luster thanks to the forward march of technology and commercialism. Once synonymous with the impossible, Mt. Everest has been a high-priced tourist attraction for decades. There are so few first ascents left of the major mountains, many of these left unsummited out of respect for the religions and cultures of those living around them, that extreme mountaineers are left pushing their goal posts further and further into danger, looking for some way to make their mark on history long after the Golden Age Of Alpinism has ended. At this intersection of human striving, late capitalism, and the films that toe the line between recording and exploiting these adventurers, The Last First: Winter K2 compellingly documents the disparate parties pursuing the final frontier for extreme mountaineering.


If you were thrilled to get sweaty palms throughout Free Solo, The Last First: Winter K2 will make your blood run cold. Amir Bar-Lev’s documentary, tracking the COVID-driven rush to summit K2, the world’s second-highest peak, in the winter—because summer is for cowards—The Last First locks three interlacing narrative ropes into its tight carabiner: One follows three friends, Icelander John Snorri Sigurjónsson and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara; a second sees the arrival of an expedition of Nepali Sherpas led by the brash Red Bull-sponsored celebrity Nirmal Purja; and a third arises with a large group of ill-prepared novices who paid a company to get them to the top. All these climbers are all brought together in part by the practicalities of the era: In 2021, adrenaline junkies had little to climb but the walls due to lockdown mandates, and Pakistan had just thrown open its borders.


That means that John Snorri and the Sadparas, whom Bar-Lev seems to have been initially working with, quickly saw their small venture become a race; a two-tent base camp became a small city. It also means that The Last First quickly moves from a more typical mode, where ominously vague talking heads and terrifyingly specific on-the-wall footage tell the straightforward story of a single climb, to something more shaded and relatable for those of us more likely to be sitting on the couch watching a movie about mountains than actually climbing one. It helps that seemingly everyone attempting the climb was equipped to contribute to the documentary—everyone has a GoPro and an iPhone; half of them hired their own cameramen. This adds yet another layer of insight to the film: Even when people die, and they do die, there are always a few people standing around, phone in hand, recording the body. It’s just one more thread—the connection between the burning modern desire to be an influencer and the ease with which a corporation, Seven Summit Treks, is able to attract clueless customers—adding uneasy depth to the adventure.


Those expecting them will still find the requisites of the genre. Harrowing nature footage—striking images of avalanches, murderous winds, and gloves careening down into the void, detached from the climber who plummeted ahead of them—and an expert’s rundown of the mechanics behind the climb make it as accessible and disturbing as these films come. But the same things that make Bar-Lev’s movie better than this also gum up its pace; just as too many climbers clogged up K2, their stories clog up The Last First. Ali’s complex relationship with the Pakistani government, the Sherpas’ desire to summit K2 as a matter of national and ethnic pride, a shoehorned love story—cobbled together from all these personal details, the narrative can get over-busy, especially when some contributors, like filmmaker Elia Saikaly, are allowed to go too long on their pet angles (like the corporate malfeasance of Seven Summit, or the scandalous rumors surrounding the Nepalese team).


It’s no wonder that this particular winter led to so many stories, but putting undue focus on some, especially when the film structures and withholds some of its information into a narrative form that feels as coy and low-rent as some Netflix true-crime, freezes up whatever tears might well up from becoming invested in any one climber’s journey. Yet, the meatheads and daredevils and pay-to-play lookie-loos form a representative and affecting unit, a group that helps illuminate the desperate, shared hunt for purpose and importance at the end of history. Taken as a whole, the faction-shattered drama between exploited tourists, reckless experts, proud pros, and the unforgiving mountain is as brutal and clear as ice.


Director: Amir Bar-Lev

Release Date: October 2, 2026 (Apple TV)

items.text:
I have 1,284 hours on record in Dota 2 on Steam. Do I regret most of them? Absolutely. Stanley Parable co-designer William Pugh recently articulated the precise reasons why.

He spoke to PC Gamer about his conflicted relationship to online multiplayer and how it’s been reflected across various games, beginning with 2005’s Worms 4: Mayhem. He was asked which Steam game he has the most hours logged in and, unsurprisingly, it’s Valve’s perennially top-performing MOBA. Pugh has 1,603 hours in Dota 2. More than even Team Fortress 2.

“It’s interesting because there’s no other game that even comes close to this volume of time,” he said. “But if you ask me, ‘Did you have a good time playing Dota 2?’ The answer is ‘no.’ The answer is ‘fuck that fucking game.’ My teammates were feeding. They weren’t supporting. When I was supporting, my carries weren’t carrying. There were people who weren’t in position. People who went too far out, people who were diving who had no business diving, people whose item picks were stupid.”

It’s a sentiment that will feel instantly recognizable to anyone who’s ever played more than a dozen hours of Defense of the Ancients 2. We feel it deep in our bones. I uninstalled the game years ago and buried the memory of it like I’d just survived a game of Jumanji. When I tease my friends about all of us re-downloading it, a dark silence engulfs the group chat.

Pugh continued:

Even thinking about it now, I’ve got to turn my fan on. I’m getting a little bit sweaty and a little bit pissed off. I’ll say it—fuck everybody who plays Dota 2. If they’re good at the game, fuck them. They’ve got no lives, and they should just get off it. It’s what started this whole AI shit. If you remember, OpenAI, one of their earliest things was they made a bot that could beat a pro.

It’s not a game made of love. It’s a game fueled by hate and a desire to conquer. It’s like chess. I played chess as a child, and there’s sweaty people who play chess. But at least you’re not playing chess with people and then when you make a mistake, they get on voice and they’re like, “Yo, this is exactly how you’re fucking up. Stop fucking up and wasting an hour of my life.”

But I was never any good, which is the saddest fucking thing. That you spend 1,600 hours of your life and you’re not actually any good at it. Goddamn, what a horrible game. I bet in your usual interviews, someone’s like, ‘I’ve spent 300 hours in this game that I love. When I had this personal tragedy, I would play this game and it helped me get through that.’ For me, it’s like, “Fuck Dota 2, I hate it.”

The thing Valve’s MOBA is best at, according to the Crows Crows Crows founder, is how much concentration it requires for players to hold all of its variables in their heads simultaneously. He likens it to being “handed a five-dimensional Rubik’s cube” that you spend an hour trying to solve. Succeed or fail, 60 minutes will have passed completely distraction-free. It quiets the brain for a spell until a groundswell of inchoate rage eventually washes it all away.

Even now, a sick part of me is still tempted to go back and play more Dota 2. Thank god my hard drive is already full.
